blocks.text: Chapter 14: What Is Good, What Is Great

inline.s: A monk asked the Buddha: “What is good? What is greatest?” The Buddha said: “One who attains the Way and guards the true is good; one whose resolve accords with the Way is greatest.”
A monk asked the Buddha: “What is good? What is greatest?” The Buddha answered: “One who attains the Way and guards the true self is most good; one whose resolve accords with the Way is greatest.”

[Attaining the Way] The wisdom by which each of the three vehicles severs delusion and realizes the principle is called the Way; practicing the three studies and producing this wisdom is called attaining the Way. [Three studies] Precepts, samadhi (concentration), and wisdom. Precepts are the prohibitions, set forth in the Vinaya collection, which prevent people from committing all evil deeds of body, speech, and mind. Samadhi is concentration, set forth in the Sutra collection, which enables people to quiet thought and clarify the mind. Wisdom is wisdom, set forth in the Abhidharma collection, which enables people to discover truth and sever ignorance. Practicing these three studies, one can attain concentration from precepts, and from concentration produce wisdom, and finally obtain the undefiled fruit of the Way; hence the three studies are also called the “three studies of no-outflow.”
[Guarding the true] The Record of the Mirror of the School says: “The gate of destroying the false self and revealing the true self.”

blocks.text: Chapter 15: What Is Power, What Is Clarity

inline.s: A monk asked the Buddha: “What has the most power? What is most clear?” The Buddha said: “Forbearance has the most power, because it harbors no evil, and is moreover peaceful and healthy. The one who is patient harbors no evil and must be honored by others. When the dust of the mind is entirely extinguished, and it is pure and without stain or blemish, this is the most clear. From before heaven and earth arose, down to the present day, all that is in the ten directions, there is nothing unseen, nothing unknown, nothing unheard; having attained omniscient wisdom, this can be called clear indeed!”

A monk asked the Buddha: “What is most powerful? What is most clear?” The Buddha answered: “Forbearance is most powerful, because it harbors no evil, and moreover brings peace and health. The patient one harbors no evil and is sure to be honored by people. When the dust of the mind is entirely extinguished, and it is pure and without stain, this is the most clear. For one whose mind-dust is extinguished, from before heaven and earth arose to the present day, all that exists in the ten directions is nothing unseen, nothing unknown, nothing unheard; having attained omniscient wisdom, this may be called the most clear!”
[Peace and health] Peace and good health. [Down to the present day] Until today. [Omniscient wisdom] The wisdom that knows all inner and outer marks of dharmas.

blocks.text: Chapter 16: Abandoning Love to See the Way

inline.s: The Buddha said: “When a person harbors love and desire and does not see the Way, it is like clear water stirred by hand — though many come to gaze, none can see their reflection. Because people’s love and desire intermingle, turbidity arises in the mind, and so they do not see the Way. You monks should abandon love and desire. When the defilement of love and desire is exhausted, the Way can be seen!”

A person harbors love and desire and therefore does not see the Way, like clear water stirred by hand — many come to be reflected, yet none can see their image in the water. It is precisely because love and desire rise and fall interwoven that the mind becomes turbid, and so one does not see the Way. You monks should abandon love and desire. When the defilement of love and desire is entirely removed, then the Way can be seen!

blocks.text: Chapter 17: When Light Comes, Darkness Departs

inline.s: The Buddha said: “One who sees the Way is like one holding a torch and entering a dark room: the darkness immediately vanishes, and the light alone remains. When one who studies the Way sees the truth, ignorance immediately vanishes, and the light remains forever!”

One who sees the Way is like holding a torch and entering a dark room: the darkness immediately vanishes, and only the light remains. When one who studies the Way realizes the truth (sees the truth), his ignorance is extinguished, and the light of his own nature remains forever!

[Seeing the truth] Realizing truth. The Shravaka Vehicle must be at least a stream-enterer before it can see the truth; a bodhisattva must be at least at the first ground before it can see the truth. [First ground] The first of the ten grounds among the fifty-two stages of the Bodhisattva Vehicle.

blocks.text: Chapter 18: Thoughts Are Equally Empty in Origin

inline.s: The Buddha said: “My Dharma is: in thought, to think the thought of no-thought; in action, to act the action of no-action; in speech, to speak the speech of no-speech; in cultivation, to cultivate the cultivation of no-cultivation. Those who comprehend are near; those who are deluded are far! The Way is cut off from words, not bound by things; a hair’s breadth of difference, and it is lost in an instant.”

The Buddha said: “My Dharma is this: to think this thought of no-thought, to practice this action of no-action, to speak this speech of no-speech, to cultivate this cultivation of no-cultivation. Those who comprehend are near the Way; those who are deluded are far from it! The ultimate truth (the Way) cannot be spoken (the Way is cut off from words), and transcends all things (not bound by things). As soon as one touches being or non-being, it is separated by heaven and earth; as soon as one enters into thought, it is no longer the Way.”
The World-Honored One revealed: thought, action, speech, and cultivation must all be free of marks and transcend being and non-being — this is the Dharma I have taught.

[Comprehend] The sense of grasping, being able to understand and penetrate the principle. [The Way cut off from words] The ultimate truth (the Way) cannot be spoken. [Not bound by things] The ultimate truth (the Way) transcends all things. [Instant] A moment; an instant.

This chapter and the second chapter’s “Within, there is nothing attained; without, nothing sought; the mind is not tied to the Way, nor does it create karma; no thought, no doing; neither practice nor realization; without passing through the stages, it is itself the supreme; this is called the Way” are both discussing the ultimate Dharma — the supreme Way.

The Essentials of the Transmission of Mind says: “Apart from all marks, living beings and Buddhas are no different; only be without thought, and that is the ultimate. If a practitioner does not directly become without thought, he may cultivate for countless kalpas and never accomplish the Way, bound by the achievements of the three vehicles and unable to gain liberation. Yet the realization of this mind has speed and slowness: some, upon hearing the Dharma in a single thought, attain no-thought; some reach the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications and then attain no-thought; some reach the ten grounds and then attain no-thought. Whether long or short, when no-thought is attained, one rests; there is nothing further to cultivate or realize. In truth there is nothing attained; this is real and not false. To attain it in a single thought and to attain it at the ten grounds are exactly equal in function, with no deeper or shallower — only through the kalpas, one has vainly endured toil.”

blocks.text: Chapter 19: Contemplating the False and the True Together

inline.s: The Buddha said: “Contemplate heaven and earth and think of impermanence. Contemplate the world and think of impermanence. Contemplate the spiritual awareness, and that is bodhi. Knowing and recognizing thus, one attains the Way swiftly!”

Contemplate heaven and earth, understanding that these are a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow. Contemplate the world, understanding that it too is a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow. Contemplate your own nature — this is enlightenment (bodhi). Knowing thus, recognizing thus, one swiftly attains the Way!
This is the contemplation that sets aside marks and returns to nature. Contemplating thus constantly, one attains the Way swiftly!

[Impermanent] That is, impermanence. [Impermanence] All dharmas are illusory and unreal, arising and ceasing in flux, not abiding even for an instant; this is called impermanence. [Spiritual awareness] That is, one’s original nature. [Bodhi] Rendered into Chinese as “enlightenment.”

blocks.text: Chapter 20: Investigating That the Self Is Empty in Origin

inline.s: The Buddha said: “One should reflect that the four great elements in the body each have their own name, and in all of them there is no self. Since there is no self at all, it is all just like an illusion!”

One should constantly reflect: the body’s flesh, skin, bones, and the five viscera and six organs, though each has its own name, once a person dies and the four elements separate, seeking a self within them one can find nothing at all. Since there is no self, what about anything else! Therefore everything is illusory.

The four great elements are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has wetness as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has movement as its nature. All tangible matter in the world possesses the four natures of solidity, wetness, warmth, and movement, hence they are called the “great” elements. For example: the body’s hair, nails, teeth, skin, bones, sinews, and flesh are the earth element of solidity; saliva, tears, pus, blood, phlegm, and other fluids are the water element of wetness; warmth and heat are the fire element of warmth; each inhalation and exhalation is the wind element of movement. Likewise, the branches and trunks of plants are the earth element of solidity; the moisture within them is the water element of wetness; absorbing nutrients from the soil to develop is the fire element of warmth; and absorbing carbon dioxide and giving out oxygen is the wind element of movement.

Once a person dies, the body rots away and is no more: bones and flesh return to earth, wetness returns to water, warmth returns to fire, and breath returns to wind. Where then is the body! So the body is not you. The Gist of Cultivating the Mind says: “When the hundred bones disintegrate, they return to fire and wind; the one thing that forever is aware (one’s own nature) covers heaven and covers earth.” That awareness which covers heaven and earth is what you truly are. Since the body is not you, what is there in the body, mind, and world built upon it to covet? What is there to resent? Life is nothing but a dream of transmigration. The first step of practice is to wake up from this dream.

blocks.text: Chapter 21: Chasing Fame and Losing the Fundamental

inline.s: The Buddha said: “People follow their emotions and desires in seeking reputation; when the reputation becomes prominent, the body is already dead! Coveting the world’s enduring fame without studying the Way, one wastes effort and exhausts the body. It is like burning incense — though people smell the fragrance, the incense has already become ashes; and the fire that endangers the body follows behind.”

People follow their own emotions and desires in pursuing fame; by the time the fame becomes prominent, the body is already dead! Coveting the world’s enduring fame without studying the Way, one wastes effort and exhausts the body in vain. Pursuing fame is like burning incense — though people smell the fragrance, the incense itself has burned to ashes! And the evil consequences of chasing fame do not end here: as you press forward in pursuit of fame, the fire that endangers this life and lives to come is burning fiercely behind you.

Where are the generals and ministers of the past and present? A heap of wild graves buried in grass” — this speaks of the emptiness of fame and rank; “to lead the yellow hound and go out the east gate — how could that ever be possible?” — this speaks of how high rank and great renown endanger the body.

[Enduring fame] The worldly name and power that people deludedly cling to, thinking it will last forever. [The fire that endangers the body] This has two meanings: first, the troubles brought by contending for fame and profit in this life; second, the troubles brought to lives to come by the karma created thereby. In truth, the greatest calamity lies in this: because one wastes energy and time pursuing fame, one delays studying the Way and realizing the Way; and by the time one can hear the Buddha’s Dharma again, who knows in what life and what world it will be! [Leading the yellow hound out the east gate] Under the Second Qin emperor, the chancellor Li Si was envied by Zhao Gao and framed, and was executed by mid-section severing at the marketplace of Xianyang, and his three clans were exterminated. Before his execution he said to his son: “I wish to join you in leading the yellow hound and going out the east gate of Shangcai to chase the cunning hare — how could that be possible!” [Three clans] The father’s clan, the mother’s clan, and the wife’s clan.

blocks.text: Chapter 22: Wealth and Beauty Bring Suffering

inline.s: The Buddha said: “As for wealth and beauty, people do not forsake them. It is like honey upon the edge of a blade — not enough for the pleasure of a single meal; yet a child licking it brings upon himself the calamity of a cut tongue.”

As for wealth and beauty, people always pursue them unceasingly. This is like the honey on a blade’s edge: there is only a little, not enough to make one meal delightful; yet a child who licks it brings upon himself the calamity of a cut tongue.

The honey on the blade” is a metaphor for wealth and beauty; the “child” is a metaphor for the foolish person who does not know what is at stake; and “the calamity of a cut tongue” is a metaphor for the evil fruits that reach to this life and the next.

blocks.text: Chapter 23: Wife and Children Are Worse Than Prison

inline.s: The Buddha said: “People are bound by wife, children, and dwellings even more than by prison. Prison has a time of release, but for wife and children one has no thought of staying far away. In passionate love for beauty, what fear is there of running about! Even with the peril of a tiger’s mouth, the mind gladly submits, casting itself into the mud and drowning itself. Therefore they are called common people. One who sees through this gate is an arhat who has left the dust of the world.”

People are bound by their wives, children, and dwellings even more cruelly than by chains and shackles in prison. Prison still has a day when the sentence is served and one is released, but one’s wife and children are never out of one’s heart. As long as there is passionate love for the opposite sex, what fear is there of toil and danger! Even at the peril of being devoured by a tiger, one gladly submits; it is like casting oneself into a bog and drowning oneself. Such a person is called a common person. If one can see through this gate, one is an arhat who has left the dust of the world.
Wife, children, and dwellings are worse than prison; the peril is the same as a tiger’s mouth, and one should quickly keep away from them.

The Buddha said: “There is no craving greater than lust. Lust as a desire has no magnitude beyond itself. Fortunately there is only this one; if there were two of the same kind, then no one under heaven could cultivate the Way.”

There is no craving of love more powerful than the craving for feminine beauty. The desire of lust is incomparably great. Fortunately this powerful desire is only one — lust; if besides it there were another desire of equally immeasurable magnitude, then no one in the world could attain the Way. (This strongly states how fierce the harm of lust is.)

In the Surangama Sutra, the Buddha said: “You cultivate samadhi, which is originally meant to transcend the dust of the world; if the mind of lust is not removed, the dust cannot be transcended. Even with much wisdom, when samadhi appears, if you do not sever lust, you must surely fall into the demonic path.”
Western Direct Pointing

Yongjia Collection on the Precepts against Lust” says: “Better to approach a venomous snake than to be intimate with a woman’s beauty. Why? A venomous snake kills a person — one death and it is over; but a woman’s beauty binds one for a hundred thousand kalpas. Every kind of torture and torment, pain without end; contemplate this deeply and reflect — it is hard to draw near. The sutra says: ‘If there were another delusion as strong as lust, no living being in all the earth would attain the Way.’”
[Torture and torment] The ancient punishment of burning at the stake. It generally refers to severe punishments, and is also used as a metaphor for unbearable suffering.

blocks.text: Chapter 25: The Fire of Desire Burns the Body

inline.s: The Buddha said: “As to love and desire for people, they are like holding a torch and walking against the wind — one is sure to suffer the calamity of burning one’s hand.”
As to people, the desire of passionate love is like holding a torch and walking against the wind — one is sure to suffer the calamity of burning one’s hand.
Western Direct Pointing

Yongjia Collection on the Precepts against Lust” says: “(A woman’s beauty) corrupts virtue and obstructs the Way; the offense is most grave. One should keep far from it, as one would avoid an enemy. Therefore the wise regard it in the thought of a venomous snake, and would rather come near a venomous snake than be intimate with a woman’s beauty.”
